overlap.title: “The book of the acts of Solomon” — what was this book, and is it the source Chronicles names?
overlap.summary: For the rest of Solomon’s acts and his wisdom, 1 Kings sends the reader to “the book of the acts of Solomon”. A phrase search of the packaged KJV finds that title in this verse only. At the same point 2 Chronicles names three other writings. The verses read do not say who wrote the book, what it held beyond the words quoted, or whether it is the same as any of the three.
overlap.reasoning: The verse names the book by a title and says what is in it: “the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom”. That much is stated. The verses read do not say who wrote it, when, or where it was kept, and the account of Solomon closes by pointing to it for what the account itself leaves out. From the next reign onward the same formula points to differently named books, “the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel” (14:19) and “of the kings of Judah” (14:29). At the matching place 2 Chronicles 9:29 points instead to “the book of Nathan the prophet”, “the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite” and “the visions of Iddo the seer”. The gap matters because the verse directs readers to another writing for additional information about Solomon, without explaining that writing’s identity or its relation to the sources named in Chronicles.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the book was a record of Solomon’s reign kept at court, distinct from the later “chronicles of the kings”; that it is the same body of writing that 2 Chronicles 9:29 cites under the names of Nathan, Ahijah and Iddo; that it was a collection that held sayings as well as deeds, in view of “and his wisdom”; that it has not survived. Limits: the two books may point to different writings for the same reign without conflict, and no conflict is asserted here; that a title is found in one verse by a phrase search does not show that the writing is not meant elsewhere under another name; whether any existing writing is this book is not something these verses settle; the Hebrew word in the title can mean “words” or “acts”, and the KJV has “acts” for it in both halves of the verse. overlap.title: Elijah is told to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha — did Elijah anoint any of them?
overlap.summary: At Horeb the Lord tells Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu king over Israel and Elisha prophet in his place. In the verses read, Elijah casts his mantle on Elisha; it is Elisha who tells Hazael he will be king; and a young prophet sent by Elisha pours oil on Jehu. The verses read report no anointing done by Elijah, and they do not say how the command given to him was carried out.
overlap.reasoning: The command is in the second person and names three acts for Elijah: “anoint Hazael”, Jehu “shalt thou anoint”, Elisha “shalt thou anoint”. The verses read report something for each of the three men. Elijah finds Elisha and casts his mantle on him, and Elisha follows and serves him (19:19–21); the verse names a mantle and does not name oil or use the word “anoint”. With Hazael it is Elisha who speaks, at Damascus, and his words are that the Lord has shown him that Hazael will be king (2 Kings 8:13); no oil and no word “anoint” stands in 8:7–15. Jehu is anointed with oil, by “one of the children of the prophets” whom Elisha sends (2 Kings 9:1–6). The command lists Hazael, Jehu and Elisha, while the account presents Elisha, Hazael and Jehu. The list does not explicitly require that the acts occur in its stated order. The gap matters because the command is the Lord’s answer to Elijah at Horeb and sets out what is to follow; the verses read do not say whether Elijah did any of the three acts himself, or by what step the task passed to Elisha.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that Elijah carried out the command through his successor, so that what Elisha did or ordered counts as done by Elijah; that “anoint” is used here for appointing or designating, so that the mantle and the spoken word answer to it; that Elijah did anoint one or more of the three in acts the books do not report; that the command was left in part undone by Elijah. Limits: the command sets no time and does not say that Elijah must act in person at each step; that an act is not reported does not show that it was not done; 2 Chronicles 22:7 says the Lord had anointed Jehu and names no human hand; the casting of the mantle is not called an anointing in the verses read, and it is not said there to be anything else.
